sources.title: Computer Vision API Pricing: What You Can Do Free, and What It Costs as You Scale
sources.text: Typically computer vision API pricing pages answer one question: what does a single call cost? That matters, but it isn't the full picture most teams need to know when they decide whether a project is affordable. You want to know what you can test for free, what the first few months will cost, and whether the bill stays reasonable once a model runs on every camera. Now that all plans have access to private projects and data for free, it is easier than ever for businesses to get started with Roboflow. This guide walks through the computer vision cost of a Roboflow project at three stages: free, getting started, and at scale. Every number comes from Roboflow's published credit rates, and we show the math so you can redo it for your own volumes. For the story behind the September 2026 pricing changes, read the launch post, Making It Easier & Cheaper to Deploy with Roboflow . This post is the practical follow-up: what those changes mean in dollars as you test and pilot, and when it's time to bring in Enterprise support. All examples use RF-DETR Nano , Roboflow's real-time vision model. On the Serverless API it costs 0.125 credits per 1,000 images. Roboflow's Core plan now starts with a Free Tier. It costs $0, needs no credit card, and includes 10 credits that refresh every month. Credits are how Roboflow meters usage: storing and labeling images, training models, and running models on Roboflow Cloud each use credits at a published rate . The Free Tier isn't a trial. It includes: The free computer vision tools are all you need for an initial POC. You can upload your own images, train a custom model, and call it from your application without entering payment details. Ten credits is easier to picture as work. Here's what 10 credits buy at Roboflow's published rates if you spend all of them on one activity: The inference math is simple: 10 credits ÷ 0.125 credits per 1,000 images = 80 × 1,000 = 80,000 images. Real projects mix these activities. Say a team wants to detect damaged boxes on a conveyor and starts with 1,000 images. A first month might look like this, using the rates on Roboflow's credits page : That leaves about 2 credits of headroom, and the 10 credits reset next month. If you run your test images on your own machine with Roboflow Inference instead of the Serverless API, the 2.5 inference credits drop to zero. These are the two questions we hear most from teams evaluating the Free Tier, so here are direct answers. Yes. Every Roboflow cloud-hosted model comes with a commercial license on every plan, including the Free Tier. If your application calls RF-DETR, YOLO26 , or any another model through the Serverless API, you can use it in a commercial product. Self-hosting is where licenses differ by model: For the details, see RF-DETR Is Free to Use Commercially and Roboflow's model licensing page . Yes. Every Core workspace, including the Free Tier, keeps projects private: your datasets and models aren't published to Roboflow Universe unless you choose to share them. Private projects aren't the same as contractual commitments. If your organization needs organizational controls and contractual commitments, such as a custom MSA or DPA, a security review (opens in a new tab) , an uptime SLA, data residency in the US or EU, or a HIPAA BAA, those require an Enterprise license. When 10 credits a month isn't enough, you can add a monthly credit pack. Each pack's total already includes your 10 free credits. Credits have a baseline price of $4, and packs cost less per credit: the bigger the pack, the lower the price per credit. The last column is 0.125 credits × the price per credit. At the $39 pack, that's 0.125 × $3.90 = about $0.49 per 1,000 images, or about $0.0005 per image. That's the computer vision cost per image at standard rates, before the per-image volume discounts covered in the next section. The $39 pack is the usual next step after a successful free test. Its 20 credits cover 160,000 RF-DETR Nano images a month, or a mix of retraining and a small pilot. Two other credit options exist: See the pricing page for current prices and Pricing & Billing in the docs (opens in a new tab) for how credits are used. Serverless API pricing is per image. Each model has a fixed credit rate per 1,000 images, whatever the image size and however long inference takes, so a forecast is images × rate. Above 250,000 images a month, per-image volume discounts apply on the Free and Core plans. They're separate from credit pack pricing. Bands count all images in your workspace for the calendar month, and each rate applies only to the images inside its band, like tax brackets. Here are the bands for RF-DETR Nano, from the Serverless API model pricing docs (opens in a new tab) : Here's what that means for monthly RF-DETR Nano model inference credits on a self-serve plan. The Credits column applies the per-image bands above, and the pack column shows the smallest monthly credit pack that covers those credits: Two separate savings show up in this table: per-image volume discounts lower the credits you use, and bigger packs lower the price of each credit. "All-in" means the full pack price divided by the images processed, so it's conservative. The credits left in each pack go to training, storage, and labeling. Past the largest pack, or once you're rolling out across sites, Enterprise adds contracted volume pricing alongside edge deployment, support, and compliance. If you're weighing this against running your own GPU instances on GCP, AWS, or Azure, our serverless GPU inference cost comparison benchmarks Roboflow Serverless against each of them. On every plan, basic self-hosted inference with the open-source Roboflow Inference package has no per-image or per-frame credit charge. You run models and Workflows on your own hardware, such as a Jetson , a Raspberry Pi , or a GPU server. Basic self-hosting is for testing, research, and getting started. sources.title: Computer Vision for Citizen Developers
sources.text: During manufacturing, defective components can slip through manual inspections. Your team knows what defective parts look like but needs a reliable way to identify them consistently. A computer vision system makes this possible by training a machine learning model on images of good and defective parts, allowing it to detect defects in new images and automate inspections across every shift. Previously, building these systems required machine learning engineers or specialized IT teams. Today, tools like Roboflow Agent and ChatGPT (opens in a new tab) make computer vision more accessible to citizen developers by allowing them to build, train, and deploy vision AI applications using natural language prompts. Across the factory floor, citizen developers are using Roboflow's computer vision tools to solve a range of challenges. Quality engineers can detect product defects before they leave the production line, safety managers can monitor PPE compliance, and operations managers can automate counting to improve inventory accuracy. Process engineers can verify assembly completeness, while production teams can automate gauge and label reading to reduce inspection errors. In this guide, you'll learn how Roboflow Agent, MCP , and ChatGPT can help you build complete vision AI applications without requiring advanced programming skills or extensive machine learning experience. Every computer vision application is built around four key components. A dataset provides the images the system learns from. Labeling marks the objects or defects in those images to teach the model what to recognize. A model learns from these examples and makes predictions on new images. Finally, deployment puts the trained model into a real-world application where its predictions can trigger actions or support decisions. Roboflow provides a no-code platform that brings those components together, allowing you to build, train, and deploy computer vision applications without writing code. Roboflow helps you build computer vision datasets with tools to collect, upload, organize, annotate, augment, and manage images and videos captured across production lines, quality inspection processes, and factory operations. These datasets can then be used to train AI models. Roboflow also helps you create and manage dataset versions. You can apply preprocessing and augmentation steps to generate new dataset versions for model training. Roboflow Annotate makes it easier to label images. Quality engineers can use its visual annotation tools to draw bounding boxes around defective products, outline damaged components, classify images, or mark specific features that an AI model can use to identify defects. When working with large datasets, manually annotating every image in Roboflow Annotate can still be time-consuming. Roboflow Auto Label helps speed up the process by using AI to automatically generate annotations. You can use Auto Label to generate bounding boxes and labels across multiple images. Quality engineers can then review the generated annotations and correct them where necessary, reducing repetitive manual work and making it easier to build large, accurately labeled datasets. Once a dataset is labeled and ready, you can use Roboflow Train to train a computer vision model to recognize patterns and identify issues in manufacturing processes. You can train models such as RF-DETR to detect product defects, identify missing components, verify assembly steps, or determine whether products meet quality standards. Roboflow Train allows you to configure training settings and start training directly within the Roboflow platform. If the model does not perform as expected, you can review incorrect predictions, add more representative images to your dataset, refine annotations, and train a new model version. This iterative process helps manufacturing teams improve model accuracy as they encounter new products, defects, and production conditions. Once your model has been trained and evaluated, you can use Roboflow Deploy to put it into production. Roboflow makes it easy to deploy models to the cloud or edge devices. With cloud deployment, you can run your models through hosted inference endpoints without managing your own inference infrastructure. For applications that require low latency, offline operation, or local processing, you can deploy models directly to edge devices on the factory floor. When you deploy a trained model as part of a Roboflow Workflow, you can combine it with other vision AI components using drag-and-drop blocks in the Workflow Editor to build complete applications. In manufacturing, you can use these workflow blocks to count defective products, trigger alerts for safety violations, and automate pass/fail decisions during quality inspections. Learn more about Roboflow Workflows (opens in a new tab) . Traditionally, building a computer vision application required coding and manually configuring each of the four components described above. Today, citizen developers can use AI agents to automate much of this process. They describe the applications they want to build using natural language, while AI agents handle the configuration and setup. Roboflow offers three ways to build computer vision applications using this approach: Roboflow Agent, the MCP Server, and the ChatGPT plugin. Roboflow Agent helps manufacturing teams build computer vision applications using natural language instead of manually configuring each step. It is a tool provided by Roboflow. Try Roboflow Agent. You can describe the problem you want to solve, such as detecting missing screws on an assembly line or identifying damaged products, and the agent will build the necessary components of your vision AI workflow to address it. Roboflow Agent can also handle other key steps in the process, including dataset preparation, model training, and workflow deployment, helping you turn your ideas into working computer vision applications without manually configuring each

stories.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

sources.name: Hugging Face
sources.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
sources.text: AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on. Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it. The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year , to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments. In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent . The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across. AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes. Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms , teams managed by an orchestrator , and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work . Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations. Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced. We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench , researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed. Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation. There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately. Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party , and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough . At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5 , announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations , where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable. With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation. sources.title: Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days
sources.text: Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol to equip its AI support agents with tools and procedures, and GPT‑6 Luna for their conversations. Beyond knowing how to answer a customer’s request, AI support agents need to be able to execute a solution. And for that, they need access to the right tools and instructions. According to Richpanel CEO Amit RG, human support agents can use 20 or 30 tools to serve a customer, and the procedures they follow may never have been written down. Richpanel ⁠ (opens in a new window) solves that using OpenAI models to both set up the tools and procedures AI support agents need to act and handle customer conversations. “The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it.” Deploying a support agent often requires a forward-deployed engineer to connect the agent to a customer’s systems and define how it should work. Amit saw that many companies didn’t have engineers to spare and asked himself, “What if that forward-deployed engineer itself was an AI agent?” So Richpanel built it: an AI manager to handle agent setup. Customers began calling it Boss AI. It writes procedures and defines how Richpanel’s frontline support agent, copilot, and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need. Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow. Richpanel designs the frontline agent to handle hundreds of thousands of conversations, making the cost of each interaction an important part of model selection. It uses GPT‑6 Luna and other OpenAI models for that work. Amit says Richpanel takes the same approach to its copilot and quality-assurance agents. “What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence,” Amit says. Richpanel’s customers may already use low-cost outsourced support. Automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point. Amit credits OpenAI with making models available that can handle long context and longer tasks while remaining cost efficient. Richpanel can use deeper reasoning to prepare its support agents and more economical models to run the conversations that follow. At the time of the October 2026 interview, Amit said Richpanel had completed approximately 300 AI customer-support deployments over the previous six months. The company guarantees customers a 50% automation rate within the first 30 days or their money back. Amit says it met that commitment across all of those deployments, adding, “In each of the cases, the AI is beating human support agents when it comes to customer satisfaction.” Product updates, practical guides, upcoming events, and more.

sources.title: Merry Making: Play, Build and Create With NVIDIA Technologies This Holiday Season
sources.text: The elves don’t have to be the only ones busy in the workshop this holiday season. With the lights twinkling and the gift wrap out, it’s the perfect time to give someone — or yourself — a spark to take a hobby to the next level. For some, that means diving into a new game. For others, it’s video editing or even building a robot. NVIDIA technologies offer something for everyone on Santa’s list. Read on to unwrap the details. With the holiday break here, everyone can be online to score bragging rights or explore a world that’s only been seen in video game trailers. For some players, an upgrade means a desktop that brings out the detail in every scene. For others, it’s a laptop they can take along when visiting family, or a way to play in the cloud on a device they already own. The right setup depends on where and what to play: For creators with a project that’s been on the backburner, the right gift this season can be the push to finally make it happen. Maybe it’s holiday clips becoming a short film, a snowy scene coming together in 3D or a livestream that brings friends across time zones to the same virtual table. Creators can use NVIDIA systems — such as GeForce RTX 50 Series and RTX Spark devices — to keep up with the workflows, along with NVIDIA Studio tools and technologies for AI acceleration. Studio Drivers support video editing, 3D design and livestreaming. In supported applications, faster processing gives more room to experiment and refine. Every robot starts somewhere. This season, it could be under the tree. Building a robot is an experiment in teaching a device to see or sense its surroundings. A first project might be as simple as using a camera to identify a candy cane or a gingerbread man, then moving on to an app that probes what the camera sees. Testing brings new questions. Can the robot recognize the candy cane under twinkling lights? Can it tell a frosted gingerbread man from an unfrosted one? Each experiment leaves more to improve and explore. The NVIDIA Jetson edge AI platform provides the hardware and software to build projects like these. It combines compact computers with the NVIDIA JetPack software development kit to help makers build robots, autonomous machines and intelligent devices. A Jetson Developer Kit is a gift to explore computer vision, generative AI and multimodal robot control, with the option to add cameras and sensors suited to various projects. AI runs directly on the device, processing information from its surroundings. When ready to take a prototype further, production systems powered by Jetson modules provide a path to deployment. See how Microduck comes to life with NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super , bringing together robot movement, visual understanding and natural-language interaction. With Hermes Agent and NVIDIA Cosmos, developers can explore how AI connects everyday requests with actions in the physical world. Bring an SO-101 arm to life with NVIDIA Jetson Orin and explore agentic robotics. Give OpenClaw a simple request, and watch it plan the steps, call NVIDIA tools and check the results. OpenShell runs the agent securely in a sandbox, controlling its access to models and robot tools. Based on ASPIRE skills, the system reuses lessons from past attempts to guide future tasks. Build a robot companion that chats, moves and understands what it sees, with NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt and Cosmos open models running locally on Jetson Orin Nano 8GB. For more advanced projects, explore vision language action models and world action models to enable increasingly sophisticated robotic behaviors — beyond simple perception and predefined actions toward understanding natural language instructions, reasoning, planning multistep tasks and interacting with the physical world. Dive into setup guides and project tutorials in Jetson AI Lab . Whether it’s a gaming upgrade, a creative project or a first robot, the right tools can open up new possibilities well beyond the holidays. Explore NVIDIA’s holiday lineup for gamers, creators and makers.
